title: From outsider to ancestor (Ruth 4)
hookLine: the Moabite woman becomes the great-grandmother of King David
tomorrow: A man in the land of Uz

lines: A MORNING AT THE CITY GATE.
cards: The book of Ruth ends with a list of names. First, a morning at the city gate, where a town did its business. Boaz sits down there, calls over a nearer kinsman of Naomi's, and gathers elders of the city as witnesses.
Naomi is selling a piece of land, he says, and you have the first right to buy it back. Sure, says the man, I'll redeem it.
Then the rest: the land comes with Ruth, the Moabite widow, and with keeping her late husband's name alive. The man backs out.
He pulls off his shoe and hands it over, the old way of sealing a deal, and the field and the future pass to Boaz.

teach.b: Notice what the book keeps calling her, right to the end: not Ruth the wife of Boaz, but Ruth the Moabitess. In chapter two she called herself a foreigner, and the story never pretends otherwise.
She marries Boaz, and a son is born. Then the camera swings to Naomi, who came home empty and asked to be called bitter.
The women of Bethlehem praise Ruth to her face, in the King James words: "thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons." Seven sons, said to a woman who buried two.
Naomi lays the baby in her lap and cares for him, and the neighbors name him: "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David."

teach.h: THE FATHER OF JESSE, THE FATHER OF DAVID.
teach.b: David. His great-grandmother came from Moab, a people the Torah elsewhere keeps out of the assembly. The rabbis noticed.
The Talmud records a reading that the old rule names Moabite men, not Moabite women, which left a door open for Ruth. The book just ends with the family line, and the last name on it is David.

Tradition reads Ruth on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah, and some readers hear why: Ruth chose to come in. A story that began with a famine and three graves ends with a cradle and a king.
She never stopped being an outsider. She became an ancestor anyway.

how: Jewish communities read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Ruth is remembered in Jewish tradition as a woman who chose to join the Jewish people and as an ancestor of King David.

o: a woman from Moab, as Ruth is always called
a woman who gleans grain in someone's field
a widow who has no sons left to care for her

games.q: the end of Ruth — tap the pairs.
p: pulls off his shoe and backs out

s: by the last chapter, the book stops calling Ruth a Moabite
she is still Ruth the Moabitess at the city gate. her origin is never erased.
it's the neighbor women who name the baby
they say a son is born to Naomi, and call him Obed.
the book of Ruth ends with King David's name
it closes with the family line, and the last name is David.

games.q: you're the nearer kinsman at the gate. you've just said yes to buying back Naomi's field. then Boaz says the field comes with Ruth the Moabitess and her late husband's name. what do you do?
o: take the field and Ruth both.
back out, and hand Boaz your shoe.
take the field and leave Ruth out of it.
games.why: he backs out and pulls off his shoe to seal it. the man who said no is never named, and the family line goes through Boaz and Ruth to David.

practice: Bring to mind someone who came into your life from somewhere else: an in-law, a stepparent, a grandparent who arrived in a new country with a suitcase, a neighbor who became family.
Ask what came into your life through them, a recipe, a word, a way of holding a baby, a reason you're here at all. If you pray, name them before God with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Moabitess, what the book keeps calling Ruth even after she becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a foreign woman, what Ruth calls herself in Ruth 2:10.
